content.text: {"what_it_is": {"claims": [{"text": "B-52 Squadrons (program element 0101113F) is a U.S. Air Force research-and-development program funded in the Research, Development, Test and Evaluation, Air Force account.", "citation": {"fact_id": "461c8a3a9de9f8bb"}}, {"text": "The program funds modernization of the B-52, a long-range bomber capable of delivering the widest variety of nuclear and conventional standoff and direct-attack munitions in the Air Force; the service plans to fly the aircraft through 2050.", "citation": {"fact_id": "11885ab4970f79f5"}}, {"text": "It sits in Budget Activity 7 (Operational System Development), the category used for development efforts that upgrade systems already fielded or approved for full-rate production.", "citation": {"fact_id": "11885ab4970f79f5"}}, {"text": "The program's largest single modernization effort is the B-52J Commercial Engine Replacement Program (CERP), which replaces the aging TF33-PW-103 engine on all 76 B-52H aircraft with new Rolls-Royce F130 commercial-derivative engines and associated subsystems; re-engined aircraft are redesignated B-52J.", "citation": {"fact_id": "2e90d22da17de437"}}, {"text": "A second major effort is the Radar Modernization Program (RMP), which replaces the legacy APQ-166 radar with the AN/APQ-188 across all 76 B-52 aircraft to overcome diminishing manufacturing sources and improve reliability for nuclear and conventional missions.", "citation": {"fact_id": "232d4456e41d025c"}}, {"text": "The program also funds communications upgrades, including Advanced Extremely High Frequency (AEHF) SATCOM integration, which replaces the aging MILSTAR terminal to provide survivable, low-probability-of-intercept two-way command-and-control communications in contested airspace.", "citation": {"fact_id": "f4744972311e99b4"}}, {"text": "Crew and training efforts include the Mission Employment Trainer, a family of reprogrammable full-crew flight simulators meant to replace antiquated legacy B-52 training devices, and the Quad Crew program, which reduces the B-52 crew from five to four by moving electronic-warfare controls to the navigator's station.", "citation": {"fact_id": "71f4e7d9c85813aa"}}]}, "why_it_matters": {"claims": [{"text": "The program's total funding is $931,164 thousand (about $931 million) requested for FY2026, down from $1,051,116 thousand enacted in FY2025.", "citation": {"fact_id": "e1c2e8009f901454"}}, {"text": "That is a year-over-year decrease of $119,952 thousand (roughly $120 million) from FY2025 to FY2026.", "citation": {"fact_id": "18fae75d2e96e128"}}, {"text": "In FY2024 the program recorded actual spending of $880,341 thousand (about $880 million), so the FY2026 request sits between the FY2024 and FY2025 levels.", "citation": {"fact_id": "de6a5641b238927d"}}, {"text": "The entire FY2026 request is discretionary funding — the R-1 exhibit shows a discretionary request of $931,164 thousand and no separate reconciliation (mandatory) request for this program element.", "citation": {"fact_id": "425ff8964df8ef1b"}}, {"text": "The money keeps a decades-old nuclear-capable bomber viable well into the future: the modernization projects address obsolescence from diminishing manufacturing sources while adding new capability that requires substantial hardware and software development and testing.", "citation": {"fact_id": "11885ab4970f79f5"}}, {"text": "Connectivity investments such as the Resilient Operational Capability Suite (ROCS) connect the B-52 to the Air Force Battle Management Network, adding resilient beyond-line-of-sight capability and an open computing environment for faster integration of future capabilities like M-code GPS and alternate navigation.", "citation": {"fact_id": "c36616a1c44672bf"}}]}, "players": {"claims": [{"text": "The program is run by the U.S. Air Force, with funding drawn from the Research, Development, Test and Evaluation, Air Force appropriation.", "citation": {"fact_id": "461c8a3a9de9f8bb"}}, {"text": "Air Force Global Strike Command is the operational command that will employ the modernized aircraft and drives program decisions — for example, in November 2024 it placed Phase II of the Quad Crew program on hold indefinitely over operational utility, fiscal constraints, and production-device availability.", "citation": {"fact_id": "bcc8b2bbf21badc1"}}, {"text": "Developmental testing and sustainment of the B-52 test fleet is supported at the Air Force Test Center at Edwards AFB, California, with depot-maintenance support for test-aircraft modifications at Tinker AFB, Oklahoma.", "citation": {"fact_id": "58eb25e3c1bafbce"}}]}, "recent_developments": {"claims": []}}
